new_statements.quote: atendiendo á los acentos graves ò agudos, pronunciarán con el tono propio de este idioma. El acento agudo es para alargar la sílaba, levantando el tono; y el grave, para abreviar bajando el tono, por ejemplo la voz uno en mixteco hín, y la nieve hìn. [...] Las vocales dobles se atenderán á los acentos graves y agudos con que se noten, para subir ó bajar el tono.
new_statements.translation: attending to the grave or acute accents, they will pronounce with the tone proper to this language. The acute accent is for lengthening the syllable, raising the tone; and the grave, for shortening it, lowering the tone, for example the word 'one' in Mixtec hín, and 'snow' hìn. [...] Double vowels are to be read according to the grave and acute accents with which they are marked, to raise or lower the tone.

new_statements.check: not checked by the second reader
new_statements.relation_note: Explicit pre-modern statement that the language has distinctive 'tono' marked by acute (raise) and grave (lower) accents, with a minimal pair; also describes h (soft aspiration/retraction), prenasalised nd, tn, affricates tz/dz and clean vowels. No stress statement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: For 1837 'Mixteca Baja' (Huajuapan/Acatlán-parish) Mixtec: the orthography marks pitch with two diacritics — acute = syllable lengthened with raised tone, grave = syllable shortened with lowered tone (minimal pair hín 'uno' vs hìn 'nieve'); double vowels carry acute/grave marks 'para subir ó bajar el tono'. Nothing is said about word stress as such.
new_statements.exceptions: none; dialect differences noted only for segments (Dzútu 'Padre' in Montañez vs Dútu in Bajo)
new_statements.identity_note: HISTORICAL (1837). Written for the 'dialecto Bajo' = the Mixtec of the Huajuapan and Acatlán parishes of the Puebla diocese, with variants noted for the 'dialecto Montañez' (Silacayoapan, Tonalá, Tlapa) (Smith 2017: 105, 114). The mxa towns (Santos Reyes Yucuná, San Simón Zahuatlán, San Miguel Amatitlán, Guadalupe Portezuelo) are among the surviving Mixtec-speaking communities of those Huajuapan-district parishes, but the book names no town, Huajuapan/Acatlán themselves no longer speak Mixtec, and other survivors of the area carry other codes (Cacaloxtepec mih, southern Puebla mit, Silacayoapan mks); so it cannot be assigned to nort2986 rather than to a neighbouring or extinct variety.

sources.note: No descriptive references for nort2986 (only Josserand 1983, Egland et al. 1983, Auderset et al. 2023); title searches return zero hits for this variety (the 42 'Yucun' hits are Arawakan Yucuna or Yucunany Mixtepec Mixtec). Glottolog places San Simón Zahuatlán under Silacayoapan Mixtec (sila1250), not nort2986.

sources.note: No stress statement for this variety (only remarks on Diuxi and Peñoles tone notation). SM2 Table 1 lists the three mxa towns among Josserand's 1977-78 survey points: amat11 San Miguel Amatitlán, guad11 Guadalupe Villahermosa (El Portesuelo)/Guadalupe Portezuelo, zahu11 San Simón Zahuatlán [sans1274]; Table 4 shows Josserand's Amatitlán wordlist ('amat') has 0% tone-marked entries. The CLDF language table assigns no variety to nort2986 (Zahuatlán is filed under Glottolog dialect sans1274 of Silacayoapan Mixtec sila1250).
